newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Police question Netanyahu in corruption probe.
newsitem.headline: Police question Netanyahu in corruption probe.

text.p: Police questioned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for more than four hours about alleged government corruption in the short-lived appointment of an attorney-general.

The Israeli leader also faced a challenge on Tuesday from the United States over his government's plans to speed up the building of roads in and around Arab East Jerusalem, which Palestinians want to make the capital of a future state.

Police went to the prime minister's office to ask him about Israel TV allegations that lawyer Roni Bar-On was named attorney-general last month in exchange for Shas party leader Arye Deri's support of Netanyahu's Hebron deal with the PLO.

"As was expected, the prime minister cooperated, told what he knew and answered all our questions," Sando Mazor, head of the national police investigative division, said to reporters after he and two other officers questioned Netanyahu.
"If the need arises to pose additional questions to the prime minister, it will be carried out in coordination with (his) complicated schedule."
The television has also alleged that Bar-On promised Deri, on trial for the past three years on corruption charges, a plea-bargain that would have let him continue his political career.
Bar-On quit on the same day he took office amid allegations by jurists and politicians he was a judicial lightweight. Israeli troops pulled out of most of Hebron last month.
Netanyahu, Bar-On and Deri have denied any wrongdoing.

On the diplomatic front, Netanyahu drew criticism from the the United States over a decision by a ministerial committee on Jerusalem to accelerate the construction and planning of access and ring roads around East Jerusalem.
"We would have preferred that the action just taken by the Israeli government not have been taken at this time," State Department spokesman Glyn Davies said.
"We've said to both parties since the Hebron agreement that they should act in ways which build confidence and enhamce prospects for future progress," he told a news briefing.

Despite the road-building decision, Netanyahu on Tuesday postponed debate for at least a week on another controversial project to build 6,500 homes for Jews on a forested hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem in the West Bank.
Davies declined coment on the so-called Har Homa project.

Critics of the plan said it would spark Palestinian rage that could prove more costly than gun battles in which 61 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed last year after Netanyahu opened a new entrance to a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.
"We are talking about a 'tunnel' that will be longer, darker and more dangerous," Yossi Sarid, a leader of the left-wing Meretz party, said about Har Homa.

Netanyahu denied on Tuesday having pledged to freeze the project in talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton at the White House last week. However, he refrained from stating when a decision might be taken.
Asked what would happen if Netanyahu cancelled the Har Homa construction, Jewish settler leader Pinchas Wallerstein told Israel Radio: "Then there will be no coalition".

Netanyahu planned to discuss Har Homa in separate meetings scheduled for Wednesday with leaders of the main opposition Labour party and the heads of factions in his ruling coalition, political sources
